reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Represents the milder allelic counterpart of Menkes disease, both caused by pathogenic variants in the copper-transporting ATPase gene ATP7A
The eponymous feature is symmetrical wedge-shaped exostoses arising from the occipital bone at the attachment of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, often palpable and visible on skull radiographs
Connective-tissue laxity dominates the phenotype: lax redundant skin (cutis laxa), joint hypermobility, hernias, and bladder diverticula prone to rupture and recurrent infection
Reflects deficient activity of copper-dependent enzymes, particularly lysyl oxidase, which impairs collagen and elastin cross-linking
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin are typically low, mirroring the biochemistry of Menkes disease but with better survival
Cognition is usually only mildly affected, in contrast to the severe neurodegeneration of classic Menkes disease
Autonomic dysfunction (chronic diarrhoea, orthostatic hypotension) and vascular tortuosity may occur
Management is supportive; parenteral copper supplementation has limited proven benefit once connective-tissue disease is established
reference.pathophysiology: Occipital horn syndrome arises from partial-loss-of-function variants in ATP7A, an X-linked gene encoding a copper-transporting P-type ATPase that delivers copper to the secretory pathway and exports it from enterocytes. Because some residual transporter activity is preserved, the phenotype is milder than the near-complete loss seen in classic Menkes disease. Impaired copper delivery limits the activity of copper-dependent cuproenzymes; reduced lysyl oxidase function in particular disrupts cross-linking of collagen and elastin, producing the lax skin, joint laxity, bladder diverticula, vascular tortuosity, and the characteristic occipital exostoses. Deficiency of other cuproenzymes such as dopamine beta-hydroxylase contributes to autonomic features, while relative sparing of central copper delivery explains the comparatively preserved neurodevelopment.
additionalDifferentials: Classic Menkes disease (more severe ATP7A phenotype)
Autosomal recessive and dominant cutis laxa syndromes
Marfan syndrome and other heritable connective-tissue disorders
additionalInvestigations: Skull and skeletal radiographs demonstrating occipital horns and other dysplastic changes
ATP7A molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Imaging of the urinary tract for bladder diverticula and hydronephrosis
Vascular imaging where arterial tortuosity or aneurysm is suspected
Autonomic function assessment including orthostatic blood pressure
redFlags: Bladder diverticulum rupture presenting as acute abdomen or urosepsis
Symptomatic arterial aneurysm or dissection from vascular fragility
Recurrent complicated urinary tract infection with obstruction
Severe orthostatic hypotension causing syncope and injury
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is substantially better than in classic Menkes disease, with survival into adulthood; morbidity stems from connective-tissue complications such as bladder diverticula, hernias, autonomic dysfunction, and occasional vascular events.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the connective-tissue phenotype as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and missing the underlying copper-transport defect
Overlooking the diagnostic occipital exostoses on imaging
Assuming copper supplementation will reverse established connective-tissue disease
Failing to monitor the urinary tract for diverticula and obstructive complications
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: No proven disease-modifying therapy; parenteral copper-histidine substitution is of limited value because it does not correct the underlying lysyl-oxidase-dependent connective-tissue defect, so care is predominantly supportive
Physiotherapy, joint protection and orthopaedic input for hypermobility, with surgical repair of hernias and symptomatic occipital exostoses
Urological surveillance for bladder diverticula and hydronephrosis, prompt antimicrobial treatment of recurrent urinary infections, and surgical repair of diverticula at risk of rupture
Management of dysautonomia and orthostatic hypotension with lifestyle measures and a noradrenaline-precursor agent where dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency causes symptomatic hypotension
Vascular surveillance for arterial tortuosity and aneurysm, with referral for intervention on significant lesions
Multidisciplinary follow-up coordinated by metabolic medicine with urology, orthopaedic and vascular input
Genetic counselling and carrier testing for the X-linked ATP7A variant, with screening of at-risk relatives
